chapter: Long Island years and Battle's estate
title: Steady salary at Moby Dick's and the social security story
summary: It was his first straight-salary job: scale plus five percent of the cash registers, and he paid the owner's social security taxes.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Oh yeah, because this was the first job I ever worked for straight salary other than the West End. I worked for salary, but I sat down and (inaudible). I say, now,

I want the union scale and I want five percent of the three cash registers (inaudible). See, (inaudible), band, too and the boss, too. But then he went up to four bartenders and a lot of times, one o'clock. Bartenders can't __________ no more. They're too tired. Now, you fellas, if you want to listen to the music, stand here and listen to the music. (Unintelligible) we ain't got no more beer. We ain't got no more whiskey. That's the way it was.

So Slick Jones bought him all brand new furniture and the guys would walk out of there on weekends with $200 extra and like that, for the three days, and walk out with it. So the boss didn't want to pay no social security and withholding, so I paid it and paid it for him, too. He called me one day and say, "What (inaudible)? I got credit for $9,000 social security." I say, "I went on and paid it, because I know you, __________." He was a brother to the federal __________ and he (inaudible). So the place went until it burned down and then they built it back up and they sold it to another fella from Florida, but he say, "I'll buy it on the terms that I get a contract that Eddie Durham would be here at least two years."
